author: nagarjuna
period: Commonly placed around the 2nd century CE; dates are uncertain
summary: Nagarjuna's foundational verses of the Madhyamaka ("Middle Way") school, arguing that all things are empty of intrinsic nature.
whyRead: It is among the most influential works of Buddhist philosophy, shaping Mahayana thought across India, Tibet and East Asia. Its arguments against fixed essences are rigorous and still debated by philosophers.
questions: Do things have an intrinsic nature of their own?
How can there be causation, motion or selfhood without fixed essences?
How do conventional and ultimate truth relate?

keyTeachings.title: Emptiness of intrinsic nature
keyTeachings.text: Nagarjuna argues that nothing has svabhava, an intrinsic, independent nature. Everything is empty (shunya) of such existence.

keyTeachings.title: Emptiness is dependent origination
keyTeachings.text: Emptiness is not a nothingness: it is identified with dependent origination (pratityasamutpada). Things exist dependently, which is why they lack independent essence.

keyTeachings.title: The two truths
keyTeachings.text: The Buddha's teaching is said to rest on two truths: conventional truth and ultimate truth. The ultimate is taught by relying on the conventional.

keyTeachings.title: Critique by consequences
keyTeachings.text: Chapter by chapter, Nagarjuna examines causation, motion, the self, time and even nirvana, showing that treating them as having fixed essences leads to contradiction.

keyTeachings.title: Samsara and nirvana
keyTeachings.text: In a much-discussed verse he states that there is not the slightest difference between samsara and nirvana, understood in terms of emptiness.

keyTeachings.title: Within Buddhist diversity
keyTeachings.text: Madhyamaka is one Mahayana school; Theravada, Abhidharma schools and Yogacara offer different analyses, and Madhyamaka itself divided into later sub-schools.

structure.label: 27 chapters, about 450 verses
structure.note: The last two chapters address the twelve links of dependent origination and philosophical views

structure.label: Commentaries
structure.note: Including those of Buddhapalita, Bhaviveka and Chandrakirti
